                                      PROJECT NO. 58482

 PROJECT NO. 58482, LARGE LOAD                    §              BEFORE THE
 DEMAND MANAGEMENT SERVICE                        §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
                                                  §               OF TEXAS

                ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY’S RESPONSE
      TO COMMISSION STAFF’S FIRST SET OF QUESTIONS FOR COMMENTS

       Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) timely files this response to the request

for comments from Staff (“Staff”) of the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”)

issued in this project on March 23, 2026. Oncor appreciates the opportunity to assist with Staff’s

efforts to adopt new rules that implement Senate Bill 6 (“SB 6”).

                   I.   RESPONSES TO QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

1. Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or a seasonal
   service, which is the better option to implement PURA § 39.170(b) and why?
       Oncor recommends that the new service be administered seasonally. A seasonal approach

is more likely to provide ERCOT certainty regarding the amount of curtailable large load capacity

available to deploy during an emergency. Unlike an as-needed approach, a seasonal approach

allows ERCOT to procure large load demand reduction capacity months in advance of any

emergency event and it ensures the availability of procured capacity throughout an entire season.

An as-needed approach, where ERCOT would issue a Market Notice to procure demand reduction

capacity in the days leading up to each potential emergency event, would give ERCOT little ability

to predict, or ensure it has a set amount of, the curtailable capacity ready for an approaching event.

A seasonal approach would give ERCOT the time and visibility necessary to procure capacity for

particularly constrained or under-procured areas, which would increase ERCOT’s ability to

respond to localized emergency conditions. As highlighted in the slides attached to Staff’s

questions, ERCOT has successfully administered Emergency Response Service (“ERS”) as a




     ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S REQUEST FOR COMMENTS – PAGE 1 OF 10
 seasonal service. ERCOT should look to the ERS procurement process as a model for this new

service.

       ERCOT should have load demand reduction capacity ready to respond to emergency

conditions at any point during a year. To achieve this, the rule should specifically require ERCOT

to implement a four-season approach to procuring large load demand reduction capacity, as

opposed to a seasonal approach that only covers the peak summer and winter months. Emergency

conditions can occur during shoulder months, when generation capacity is lower due to increased

generation facility planned outages for annual maintenance.

2. PURA § 39.170(b) states the commission must require ERCOT to develop a reliability
   service to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency condition. PURA §
   39.170(b)(1) states the rules governing the new service must specify the periods when
   the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme weather
   events.

           a. Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances
              other than extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?

       Yes. The language of PURA § 39.170(b)(1), which requires that the Commission’s rule

“specify the periods when the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during

extreme weather events,” should not be read to limit the general language found in PURA §

39.170(b), which states that the service is “to be deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency

condition.” Further, none of the specific parameters included in PURA 39.170(b)(1)-(3) should

limit the Commission’s interpretation of “emergency condition.” Consistent with Oncor’s and

ERCOT’s comments in Docket No. 58479, Oncor recommends that an “emergency condition”

should align with the definition of “emergency condition” included in the ERCOT Protocols: “[a]n

operating condition in which the safety or reliability of the ERCOT System is compromised or




     ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S REQUEST FOR COMMENTS – PAGE 2 OF 10
 threatened, as determined by ERCOT.” 1 Importantly, this definition must not be limited to a

system-wide Energy Emergency Alert event or an extreme weather event—an “emergency

condition” must also include anticipated regional or localized emergencies.                     Along with

compromising grid reliability in the immediate area, regional and localized emergency conditions

can cascade into system-wide emergency conditions if not mitigated quickly. ERCOT should be

able to rely on the new service to address each of these types of emergencies.

            b. Should the commission define “extreme weather event” and, if so, how
               should it be defined?
        No. There is no need to define the term “extreme weather event” in this rule. The

Commission should promote operational flexibility by allowing ERCOT to define that term in its

Protocols as it implements the new rule. This approach means ERCOT could appropriately adjust

the definition to meet future operational realities without a Commission rulemaking.

3. PURA § 39.170(b)(3) states the rules governing the new service must prohibit
   participation by any large load customer that curtails in response to the wholesale price
   of electricity, as determined by ERCOT, or that otherwise participates in a different
   reliability or ancillary service. PURA § 37.0561(e)—which allows ERCOT to direct a
   large load customer with onsite backup generation to either curtail its load or deploy its
   backup generation under certain circumstances—states that a large load customer with
   onsite backup generation may participate in a service authorized by PURA § 39.170(b).

            a. What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load
               customer 24 hours to ramp down safely?
        Oncor elects not to respond to Question No. 3(a).

            b. What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b), if any, should
               apply to participation in the new service?
        Oncor elects not to respond to Question No. 3(b).




         1
           Rulemaking for Net Metering Arrangements Involving a Large Load Co-Located with an Existing
Generation Resource Under PURA § 39.169, Docket No. 58479, Oncor’s Reply Comments on the Commission’s
Proposal for Publication of New 16 TAC §25.205 (Oct. 31, 2025) at 4-5; Docket No. 58479, Electric Reliability
Council of Texas, Inc.’s Responses to Commission Questions and Comments Regarding Proposed 16 TAC § 25.205
(Oct. 17, 2025) at 6; ERCOT Nodal Protocols Section 2.1.


      ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S REQUEST FOR COMMENTS – PAGE 3 OF 10
            c. Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as
              four coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude participation
              in the new service?

       The rule should not allow the participation in the new service of any portion of a large

load’s curtailable capacity that is responsive to power prices or otherwise already allocated to

another demand response service. ERCOT needs to be assured that the demand reduction capacity

it procures through the new service will be available for dispatch during emergency events and

will not have already curtailed based on price responsiveness or on the dispatch of another service.

Otherwise, this kind of double dipping will only compromise ERCOT’s ability to respond to

emergency conditions. However, even if a portion of a large load’s capacity is price responsive or

already allocated, it should be permitted to offer the remaining, unallocated portion of its load as

demand reduction capacity under the new service. Put simply, a large load that participates in the

new service must be capable of meeting its obligations when called upon by ERCOT.

           d. Should the commission define “curtailment in response to wholesale price of
              electricity” and, if so, how should it be defined?

       Oncor elects not to respond to Question No. 3(d).

4. How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service?

       Oncor elects not to respond to Question No. 4.

5. What additional information should the Commission consider in its implementation of
   PURA § 39.170(b)?
       First, Oncor recommends that the Commission consider, either in this rulemaking or in a

separate rulemaking, the implementation of PURA §37.0561(e), which requires ERCOT to

“establish a threshold before or during an energy emergency alert at which the organization may

issue reasonable notice that large load customers with on-site backup generating facilities may be

directed to either deploy the customer’s on-site backup generating facilities or curtail load.” This

same section allows ERCOT to “direct the applicable electric utility or municipally owned utility


     ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S REQUEST FOR COMMENTS – PAGE 4 OF 10
 to require the large load customer to either deploy the customer’s on-site backup generation

facilities or curtail load.” Oncor recommends that each large load that meets the on-site backup

generating facilities criteria in PURA §37.0561(e) be required to register with ERCOT and install

remote systems that allow the large load to be dispatched or controlled by the Security-Constrained

Economic Dispatch (“SCED”) process.

       While TSPs, like Oncor, have a limited ability to contact and remotely disconnect large

load customers, they have no control over whether the customer actually curtails short of opening

the main breaker at the site. Completely disconnecting the large load does not allow for the partial

curtailment of large loads participating in the new service. Also, a utility-controlled complete

disconnection of participating large loads would compromise the efficient dispatch of net metering

arrangements or large loads with backup generators that can export to the ERCOT grid because

opening breakers would disconnect any backup generation or co-located generation resource

“made available” to the grid under PURA § 39.169(d). The significant number of large loads likely

to meet the PURA §37.0561(e) criteria would make TSP coordination with individual large loads

impractical and will necessitate a centralized approach administered by ERCOT. A SCED-based

approach would also help towards meeting the requirement for ERCOT to account for deployments

under PURA §37.0561(e) when calculating any price adjustments for reliability deployments.

       Second, Oncor recommends that Staff consider and generally define the events or

conditions that trigger (i) ERCOT’s issuance of a 24-hour notice and (ii) the deployment of the

new service. Oncor generally recommends that the service be deployed prior to the firm load shed

of non-participating large loads. Staff could adopt similar general deployment language as found

in the Commission’s ERS rule at 16 TAC § 25.507(b). Oncor recommends: “the new service will

be deployed by ERCOT to help prevent or alleviate an actual or anticipated emergency condition.”




     ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S REQUEST FOR COMMENTS – PAGE 5 OF 10
 This language grants appropriate discretion to ERCOT while also creating some certainty

regarding deployment.

       Alternatively, Staff could opt to include this kind of more specific deployment trigger in

its rule. Under Section 6.5.9.4.1 of its Nodal Protocols, ERCOT has directed the deployment of

ERS resources after Voluntary Early Curtailment Load (“VECL”) and only after Physical

Responsive Capability (“PRC”) falls below 3,000 MW and is expected not to recover within 30

minutes. But Oncor recommends leaving this discretion to ERCOT.

       Third, Oncor recommends that the Commission’s rule clearly define how the 24-hour

notice required by PURA § 39.170(b)(2) will operate. PURA § 39.170(b)(2) requires that the

Commission’s new rule “ensure that [ERCOT] provides at least a 24-hour notice to large load

customers . . . .” The rule should require ERCOT to issue a 24-hour notice indicating that a

curtailment may be required when ERCOT determines that an emergency condition or EEA event

is probable. The rule should give ERCOT the ability to issue the 24-hour notice without requiring

that it actually deploy the service; the rule should give ERCOT the operational flexibility to

withdraw the notice without deploying the service. But it should be designed to minimize frequent

notices and “false alarms” by ensuring that ERCOT only issues 24-hour warnings when

deployment is relatively certain.

       Also, Staff should consider creating sub-categories of the large loads participating in the

new service, grouped based on how far in advance each load must receive notice before it can

curtail. Many loads require far less time than 24-hours’ notice to curtail and should be operated

commensurate to their ability to speedily curtail and should be compensated for their increased

flexibility. ERCOT has already implemented a similar grouping system by dividing ERS resources




     ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S REQUEST FOR COMMENTS – PAGE 6 OF 10
 into those that require 10 minutes of notification (ERS-10) and those that require 30 minutes (ERS-

30).

        Fourth, Staff should carefully consider how the new service interacts with other large load

curtailment requirements and services, including VECL and ERS. Oncor recommends that the

rule be drafted so that the new service is complementary to and compatible with these services.

Oncor recommends that the new rule ensure that the new service be sufficiently distinct from these

existing services. Further, the Commission should consider how the new service may interact or

align with any future executive orders like the recent Department of Energy Order No. 202-26-

01A issued during Winter Storm Fern in January 2026, which authorized ERCOT to direct the

deployment of backup generation resources at large loads.

        Fifth, Oncor recommends that the rule allocate curtailment responsibility solely to the large

loads that are dispatched by ERCOT under the new service. The Qualified Scheduling Entity

(“QSE”) of a given participating large load should not be able to transfer curtailment obligation

from a dispatched load to other participating large loads in its portfolio. Oncor recommends that

load reduction under the new service be location and load specific. Allocating or transferring

curtailment obligations from one load to another in a different geographic area could frustrate

ERCOT’s ability to respond to localized emergency conditions.

        Finally, Oncor recommends that the Commission provide guidance on which entities are

specifically responsible for ensuring curtailment in the case that ERCOT dispatches demand

reduction capacity. Transmission Service Providers (“TSP”), like Oncor, do not have control over

the specific extent to which a large load curtails. TSPs are able to open the breaker at a large load

site or keep it closed. Oncor recommends that the rule require that curtailment under the new

service be dispatched by ERCOT via SCED. The rule should also contemplate that large load




       ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S REQUEST FOR COMMENTS – PAGE 7 OF 10
 customers will receive this SCED dispatch through their QSEs, and that curtailment is ultimately

the responsibility of participating large loads.

6. PURA §39.170(a) states: The commission shall require the independent organization
   certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region to ensure that each electric
   cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally owned utility serving
   a transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol, including the installation of any
   necessary equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected, to allow the
   load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric cooperative, transmission and
   distribution utility, or municipally owned utility shall confer with the customer to the
   extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated manner. This subsection applies only to a
   load interconnected after December 31, 2025, that is not: (1) Load operated by a critical
   load industrial customer, as defined by Section 17.002; or (2) Designated as a critical
   natural gas facility under Section 38.074. Should the Commission include in this
   rulemaking a directive implementing PURA §39.170(a)?

       For the reasons outlined in Oncor’s response to Question No. 5, above, Oncor recommends

that the new rule require each large load to which PURA § 39.170(a) applies to register with

ERCOT and install remote systems that allow all large loads, both those that participate in the new

service and those that do not, to be dispatched or controlled by ERCOT through a centralized

SCED process. Oncor notes that ERCOT has already promulgated a requirement that each large

load install a remote-control breaker configuration capable of isolating the large load from the grid

in ERCOT Planning Guide Section 9.2.5. But the Commission should add language to its rule to

strengthen that requirement by requiring SCED-integrated load curtailment equipment be installed

at each large load to facilitate centralized, remote operability.

                                      II.   CONCLUSION

       Oncor appreciates the opportunity to assist with Staff’s evaluations pursuant to SB 6.




     ONCOR’S RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S REQUEST FOR COMMENTS – PAGE 8 OF 10

its rule. Under Section 6.5.9.4.1 of its Nodal Protocols, ERCOT has directed the deployment of

ERS resources after Voluntary Early Curtailment Load ("VECL") and only after Physical

Responsive Capability ("PRC") falls below 3,000 MW and is expected not to recover within 30

minutes. But Oncor recommends leaving this discretion to ERCOT.

       Third, Oncor recommends that the Commission's rule clearly define how the 24-hour

notice required by PURA § 39.170(b)(2) will operate. PURA § 39.170(b)(2) requires that the

Commission's new rule "ensure that [ERCOT] provides at least a 24-hour notice to large load

customers ...." The rule should require ERCOT to issue a 24-hour notice indicating that a

curtailment may be required when ERCOT determines that an emergency condition or EEA event

is probable. The rule should give ERCOT the ability to issue the 24-hour notice without requiring

that it actually deploy the service; the rule should give ERCOT the operational flexibility to

withdraw the notice without deploying the service. But it should be designed to minimize frequent

notices and "false alarms" by ensuring that ERCOT only issues 24-hour warnings when

deployment is relatively certain.

       Also, Staff should consider creating sub-categories of the large loads participating in the

new service, grouped based on how far in advance each load must receive notice before it can

curtail. Many loads require far less time than 24-hours' notice to curtail and should be operated

commensurate to their ability to speedily curtail and should be compensated for their increased

flexibility. ERCOT has already implemented a similar grouping system by dividing ERS resources

 into those that require 10 minutes ofnotification (ERS-10) and those that require 30 minutes (ERS-

30).

        Fourth, Staff should carefully consider how the new service interacts with other large load

curtailment requirements and services, including VECL and ERS. Oncor recommends that the

rule be drafted so that the new service is complementary to and compatible with these services.

Oncor recommends that the new rule ensure that the new service be sufficiently distinct from these

existing services. Further, the Commission should consider how the new service may interact or

align with any future executive orders like the recent Department of Energy Order No. 202-26-

01A issued during Winter Storm Fern in January 2026, which authorized ERCOT to direct the

deployment ofbackup generation resources at large loads.

        Fifth, Oncor recommends that the rule allocate curtailment responsibility solely to the large

loads that are dispatched by ERCOT under the new service. The Qualified Scheduling Entity

("QSE") of a given participating large load should not be able to transfer curtailment obligation

from a dispatched load to other participating large loads in its portfolio. Oncor recommends that

load reduction under the new service be location and load specific. Allocating or transferring

curtailment obligations from one load to another in a different geographic area could frustrate

ERCOT's ability to respond to localized emergency conditions.

        Finally, Oncor recommends that the Commission provide guidance on which entities are

specifically responsible for ensuring curtailment in the case that ERCOT dispatches demand

reduction capacity. Transmission Service Providers ("TSP"), like Oncor, do not have control over

the specific extent to which a large load curtails. TSPs are able to open the breaker at a large load

site or keep it closed. Oncor recommends that the rule require that curtailment under the new

service be dispatched by ERCOT via SCED. The rule should also contemplate that large load

 customers will receive this SCED dispatch through their QSEs, and that curtailment is ultimately

the responsibility of participating large loads.

6. PURA §39.170(a) states: The commission shall require the independent organization
   certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region to ensure that each electric
    cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally owned utility serving
    a transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol, including the installation of any
    necessary equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected, to allow the
    load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric cooperative, transmission and
    distribution utility, or municipally owned utility shall confer with the customer to the
    extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated manner. This subsection applies only to a
    load interconnected after December 31, 2025, that is not: (1) Load operated by a critical
    load industrial customer, as defined by Section 17.002; or (2) Designated as a critical
    natural gas facility under Section 38.074. Should the Commission include in this
    rulemaking a directive implementing PURA §39.170(a)?

       For the reasons outlined in Oncor's response to Question No. 5, above, Oncor recommends

that the new rule require each large load to which PURA § 39. 170(a) applies to register with

ERCOT and install remote systems that allow alllarge loads, both those that participate in the new

service and those that do not, to be dispatched or controlled by ERCOT through a centralized

SCED process. Oncor notes that ERCOT has already promulgated a requirement that each large

load install a remote-control breaker configuration capable of isolating the large load from the grid

in ERCOT Planning Guide Section 9.2.5. But the Commission should add language to its rule to

strengthen that requirement by requiring SCED-integrated load curtailment equipment be installed

at each large load to facilitate centralized, remote operability.
